content: YY1, also known as Yin Yang 1, is a transcriptional repressor protein in humans encoded by the YY1 gene. It is a ubiquitously expressed transcription factor that belongs to the GLI-Kruppel class of zinc finger proteins. This protein plays a dual role in gene regulation, as it can both repress and activate a wide variety of gene promoters. The name Yin Yang reflects its dual functionality. YY1 exerts its regulatory effects by recruiting histone deacetylases (HDACs) or histone acetyltransferases (HATs) to specific promoters, thereby modulating histone modifications to either repress or activate transcription. Additionally, YY1 facilitates the formation of chromatin loops between enhancers and promoters by forming dimers and promoting DNA interactions. Disruption of YY1 function can lead to the breakdown of these enhancer-promoter loops, resulting in altered gene expression. Clinically, mutations in the YY1 gene, including heterozygous deletions, missense mutations, and nonsense mutations, are associated with Gabriele-DeVries syndrome (GADEVS). This is an autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by intellectual disability, distinct dysmorphic facial features, feeding difficulties, intrauterine growth restriction, variable cognitive impairments, behavioral abnormalities, and other congenital malformations. A dedicated website exists to facilitate the sharing and collection of clinical information among healthcare professionals and families of individuals with YY1 mutations. YY1 has been shown to interact with several other proteins, including: ATF6 (Activating Transcription Factor 6), EP300 (a histone acetyltransferase), FKBP3 (FK506-binding protein 3), HDAC3 (Histone Deacetylase 3), Histone Deacetylase 2, Myc (a proto-oncogene protein), NOTCH1 (a key regulator in cell differentiation), RYBP (Ring1 and YY1 Binding Protein), and SAP30 (Sin3A-associated protein 30), as well as Seryl-tRNA synthetase. These interactions highlight the complex regulatory network in which YY1 is involved.
